new_statements.quote: Accent in Bāgandji is non-phonemic, its position is predictable and is governed by rules, but these rules are complicated by morphophonemic processes. The accent is marked not only by stress, but by a distinct rise in pitch. The basic pattern of the accent is the same as in practically all Australian languages: it falls on the first syllable of a word. Words of two syllables therefore follow a trochaic rhythm: [...] In all types of words of three syllables the accent is still on the first syllable, and the final syllable (unless it is a declensional affix or a clitic) has a very minor secondary accent (ˋ) with only a slight rise in pitch. The rhythm is therefore dactylic

new_statements.rule_in_words: Main word accent (stress + pitch rise) is predictable and falls on the first syllable of the word; each morpheme can bear only one main stress, on its initial syllable (p.33). This trochaic/dactylic pattern is the prevailing system of Guṇu and the underlying pattern of Southern Bāgandji (the dialect group that includes Bandjigali), where an additional strong rising accent falls on the juncture syllable when certain vowel-initial bound morphemes follow.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Trisyllables: very minor secondary accent on the final syllable (unless it is a declensional affix or clitic), i.e. dactylic; four-syllable words: trochaic with a more prominent secondary accent (p.45). Andersen 2015 restates this as weak secondary stress on the third syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Southern Bāgandji (pp.45-47): in two-morpheme words, if the second morpheme is vowel-initial and belongs to one of four classes (bound subject/object pronouns, possessive affixes, optative and present participle, -mbala 'with' / emphatic -ḏiŋa / singular -ulu) a strong rising accent falls on the juncture syllable; case/tense markers and stem-forming affixes do not attract it; 3pl -ŋga always attracts a rising accent to the preceding syllable; sequences of bound morphemes follow fixed (generally dactylic) patterns (II.5.4). Guṇu lacks the juncture accent. Hercus 2013 (via Andersen 2015): under strong emphasis/calling, stress shifts to the final syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent ('first syllable of a word'); p.33 frames the one-main-stress constraint per morpheme, and bound morphemes may carry their own stress/long vowel at their beginning. Description is for Bāgandji as a whole, illustrated mainly from Southern Bāgandji and Guṇu speakers; Bandjigali material (George Dutton) is included in the corpus but the accent section does not single it out. Beckett & Hercus 2009 p.92 and Beckett, Hercus & Martin 2008 p.92, both centred on Pantyikali (=Bandjigali) country/texts, restate: 'The first syllable of a word always carries the accent'.
new_statements.identity_note: band1337 'Bandjigali' is a Glottolog bookkeeping languoid (retired ISO 639-3 bjd, merged into drl Paakantyi by CR 2011-145, effective 2012). It corresponds to Pantyikali / Wanyiwalku (Hercus 1982's 'Wanjubaḷgu-Bandjigali', sec. 1.4.3 pp.10-11), which Hercus places in the Southern Bāgandji dialect group (Table 1, p.13) of the Darling River language = Paakantyi, glottocode darl1243. The quoted accent statement (Hercus 1982 II.5.3) is made for Bāgandji as a whole: the plain initial trochaic/dactylic pattern is said to be the prevailing system of Guṇu (Kurnu) and the underlying pattern of Southern Bāgandji, which adds a juncture rising accent; Bandjigali is not treated separately in the phonology, though George Dutton's Bandjigali recordings are part of the corpus. The two later restatements (Beckett, Hercus & Martin 2008 p.92; Beckett & Hercus 2009 p.92) are in works specifically about Pantyikali country/texts. A catalog entry would most naturally sit under darl1243 (Paakantyi) with band1337 as a dialect pointer.

sources.citation: Andersen, Elena Handlos. 2015. Development of a Learner's Grammar for Paakantyi. MA (Research) thesis, University of Sydney.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Learner's grammar sec. 2.2 'Stress' p.21: 'In Paakantyi, words with more than one syllable always have the main (primary) stress on the first syllable. In words with three or more syllables, there is also a weak (secondary) stress on the third syllable.' Quotes Hercus (2013:124-125) that under strong emphasis (calling) stress shifts to the last syllable. Derivative of Hercus; pan-Paakantyi, not Bandjigali-specific.
